newsitem.title: UGANDA: Iranian leader in talks with Uganda's Museveni.
newsitem.headline: Iranian leader in talks with Uganda's Museveni.

text.p: Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani and Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni began talks on Thursday after Iran signed a wide-ranging understanding with Kenya.
On the second leg of a six-nation African tour to drum up business, Rafsanjani and his delegation met Museveni in Kampala before the two leaders went into private talks, officials said.
Rafsanjani arrived in Uganda on Thursday from Kenya, where Iran offered in a memorandum of understanding to throw its weight behind Kenya's energy, industry and agricultural sectors.
Rafsanjani held a final round of talks with Kenya's President Daniel arap Moi before flying to Entebbe, Uganda.
At the end of his visit to Uganda on Sunday, Rafsanjani, who is accompanied by Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati, heads north to Sudan for talks with the Islamic-backed government in Khartoum.
Diplomats said Rafsanjani's African tour was designed to reduce Iran's international isolation and the impact of U.S. sanctions. Washington accuses Iran of sponsoring terrorism, a charge Iran denies.
Thousands of people -- many waving Ugandan and Iranian flags -- lined the road to Kampala to receive the Iranian leader.
Rafsanjani was welcomed at Entebbe airport by Museveni, who took power in 1986 and has helped lead Uganda out of economic misery and dictatorships under deposed dictators Idi Amin and Milton Obote.
Museveni would host a state dinner on Thursday night.

As well as ways to improve trade diplomats expected Museveni and Rafsanjani to discuss Uganda's chilly relations with Sudan. Uganda and Sudan accuse each other of backing rebels in each other's territory.
Rafsanjani, his wife and his 180-strong Iranian delegation meet Ugandan Moslem religious leaders on Friday and the heads of other faiths on Saturday night, Ugandan officials said.
He will also visit Islamic institutions outside Kampala on Friday to join worshippers for the day's main Islamic prayers.

Rafsanjani's African tour comes a month after U.S. President Bill Clinton tightened sanctions against Iran. The law penalises non-U.S. firms that invest $40 million or more a year in the oil and gas sectors of Iran or Libya.
Iran has steadily stepped up its diplomatic presence in Africa and tried to boost cultural and religious links with Moslems on the world's poorest continent.
But with the exception of Sudan none of the countries Rafsanjani will visit has a Moslem majority and in most of them Christianity is the main religion.
While in Kenya, Rafsanjani criticised the United States for its cruise missile attacks against Iraq, Iran's western neighbour, but said the Iraqis had provided the pretext.
The United States fired cruise missiles at Iraqi air defence targets on Tuesday and Wednesday in retaliation for Saturday's incursion by Iraqi forces into Kurdish areas in northern Iraq.
